utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We are here the remainder of the examination, that is cross-examination of the present witness in closed session. Could we turn into closed session unless there's anything to be raised in open session at this moment. Apparently not. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the representatives of the Republic of Serbia be escorted into the courtroom, and immediately after that witness JF-095. Meanwhile, I inform the parties that the Chamber has decided that the time at this moment granted for cross-examination is one hour and a half for each Defence team, and to the extent it may serve as a guidance, I'd like to inform the parties that if conclusions are written down without a proper factual basis, then it's of hardly any use to establish that there's no proper factual basis because the Chamber, of course, certainly after discussion we had last week is testing itself whether there's any factual basis or not. Then the second issue is that it may have a better impact if we are talking about authenticity of documents and to what extent it may have been overlooked to start with the strong examples so that if you are running out of time, that you are not missing the strong examples. But of course, the Chamber leaves it to the Defence teams how to conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness JF-095. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also welcome to you, the representatives of the Republic of Serbia. We have received your requests. We'll consider them, that is protective measures especially in relation to the report, and the delivery of a copy of the transcript of the closed session. We'll consider your request. Not immediately now, but you will hear our decision on the matter, and we may first want to hear what the parties' view on the matter is. Witness JF-095, first of all, thank you very much for coming back to The Hague. It's highly appreciated. It's certainly very inconvenient for you but we have to proceed and again the Chamber appreciates your flexibility. I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony and I'd like to inform you that you will be first -- that you'll be now cross-examined by the Defence teams. When I was talking about one hour and a half, I was talking about the two witnesses together. The Chamber very much would like to see whether it's possible to conclude the testimony of this witness today. Who will go first, is it the Stanisic Defence or is it the Simatovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we just have a moment, Your Honour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I shall go first, Your Honour. May I just retrieve the lectern, there was a bit of confusion between the teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness JF-095, you'll first be cross-examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to deal first of all with 65 ter 3880. And the subject I want to deal with, Mr. Witness, is the subject of whether and under what authority the Serbian DB was permitted to form any militarised unit. Do you recall your evidence concerning this last week?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you maintain that the -- is it your position -- perhaps I should put it this way, is it your position that the Serbian DB were not entitled to form a militarised unit at any stage between 1991 and 1996? Is that how I should understand your evidence thus far?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My apologies. What was it that you did say? What is your position in relation to, let's make it concrete, the formation of, say, the JATD in 1993, according to the rules and regulations in place at that time?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I've already mentioned that the RDB of the republic of Serbian MUP was a department which was part of the Ministry of the Interior. And that the internal organisation and job descriptions within that department were established by the rules on the internal organisation in accordance with the Law on the Internal Affairs Service, and that the rules or a separate decision could envisage that as part of the RDB, one such unit may be formed as a separate organisational unit, especially so as the RDB also had reserve forces at its disposal, in other words, an enlarged composition. During my answers in response to the Prosecutor's question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt you but since your answer is relatively long. Mr. Jordash, would you switch off your microphone when the witness answers the questions because of the voice distortion. Please proceed. I interrupted you. You said that "the RDB also had reserve forces at its disposal," you said, "in other words, an enlarged composition." Could you please resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can resume. In response to the Prosecutor's question whether certain unidentified individuals who were mentioned in the financial documents but were not listed as employees or members of the reserve staff, whether they could be engaged as fighters abroad. And my answer to that question was no. I am not sure, in fact, what is meant by abroad here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And is your answer to that the same if those individuals were part of a unit, an ad hoc unit, tasked with protecting the territorial integrity of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If its task was to protect the territorial integrity of Serbia, that would have been legal and legitimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'm getting a bit confused. We have two categories of people working for the RDB. The listed ones and those not listed but appearing in the financial documents. Now, it's unclear to me, the earlier question, the questions put by Mr. Groome were by the, I think by those who appear on the financial documents, not on the, I would say the regular employment list. Now, what -- now, we have since then, now, the witness has made a distinction now between abroad and protecting the territorial integrity. Your question was about the not listed persons or was it about the listed persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It was about persons who appeared in the financial document but were not listed as employees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this is how you understood the question, Witness JF-095, that those who appear in the financial documents but were not listed as employees could be used in order to protect the territorial integrity even if that would be not necessarily gathering intelligence? That is to say that beyond gathering intelligence, they might have been tasked with other tasks as well related to the protection of the territorial integrity of Serbia, and I do understand if you refer to Serbia, you are talking about the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm referring to the Republic of Serbia. In the event that its territorial integrity were endangered, it is the responsibility of every citizen of the Republic of Serbia to take part in the defence of its integrity one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I have Rule 65 ter 2375 on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to refer you, Mr. Witness, to the rules on the internal organisation of the state security department within the Ministry of the Interior, January 1992, and ask you about a particular provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we go, please, to page 4. Let's go to page 3, Article 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before I ask you questions upon this, would you please indicate your understanding of the significance of these rules concerning the operations of the state security of Serbia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was and still is one of the basic documents providing for the organisation -- internal organisation of the then RDB and what is now called the BIA. It regulates the sphere of work, tasks and duties, organisational units which form part of the department, and these rules also include as its constituent part a table of job -- different job classifications with the number of people required to work and their level of education.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at the time these rules were promulgated in 1992, would you agree with me that the federal government had issued a declaration of an a imminent threat of war in the SFRY? That declaration having been made on the 18th of October, 1981.

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying that that is a fact, although I can't answer with any degree of certainty whether that happened at the time you specify or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to testify and confirm that it had happened by 1992? It had happened at some point within 1991?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably. At this point in time, however, I'm unable to say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough. We'll leave that for further evidence. Please would you have a quick look at Article 3 of these rules, and in particular the section of Article 3 which reads, and I'll read it now: "Other republic security duties are in particular the duties of providing counter-intelligence protection to republican organs, organising and carrying out preparations for defence and work in case of an imminent threat of war, and in war, preparing appropriate contributions to the plan for the defence of the republic, planning and co-ordinating the duties of protecting facilities, areas, and work-places important for the defence of the republic, and organising and providing cryptographic data protection and special purpose communications." Would it be fair to describe that as the enabling provision which permitted the state security of Serbia to form such military units such as the JATD?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I also have on the screen, please, Rule 65 ter 4695.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. We'll move to another exhibit, or potential exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender that particular article or the rules as an exhibit, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you've drawn our attention to 3 and 4, or, I think that's what you said in the beginning, but Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to the rules being introduced. I would ask that the entire set of rules so the Chamber can read them in their full context and not just cherry-pick particular rules for particular purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Absolutely, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole set of the rules. We would like to hear whenever you introduce something in evidence whether in your view it could be made public at a later stage, yes or no. Of course, we'll also hear later the view of the Republic of Serbia. But if you already could indicate whether you think this is a document which says state secrets so therefore it might well be that one would be inclined to say that this should not be public. At the same time, we'd have to look at the content before the Chamber will decide whether there are compelling reasons to keep them confidential. Could we already assign a number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D113 is admitted into evidence and for the time being under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Witness, would you look at the document on the screen and read the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've just been told that this is already an exhibit, P559. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the witness has looked at what he is asked to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't follow Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me just check. I thought the witness would have read the first page, but he is looking at you so he expects a question, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is -- we can go to page 2 very quickly, and you will see this appears to be an order or decision by Panic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to page 1, from your experience and knowledge of the way in which the security services worked, the first paragraph of the letter or the first three paragraphs deal with or refer to various incidents giving rise to the eventual decision by Panic, including such things as armed individuals, groups, and paramilitary units crossing from the territory of BH to Sandzak or the other way around provoking various incidents, public order incidents and so on with reference to the border control and customs MUP and VJ. Would you agree with me that it is this type of activity which state security was enabled to create ad hoc armed units to deal with, incidents along the border of Serbia? Do you follow my question, I know it was a bit long? Would you agree with me that --

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. That would be a situation in which that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you, before being shown this decision by Panic, aware of a decision by the Yugoslav Army General Staff chief to allow collaboration between the MUP of Serbia and the Yugoslav Army to deal with threats to the territorial integrity of Serbia as outlined in this document?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't answer in the affirmative. It just so happens that I'm not aware of that decision. In principle, I'm a witness who is here to testify to facts regarding the reports. These questions are not for me to answer, although I don't have a problem with that, nevertheless you must bear in mind my position at the time and understand that I simply cannot answer questions such as these with any degree of certainty whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I want to be clear about what you've just said. You can answer with certainty about the enabling provision of the rules of the DB, you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your question has been interpreted accurately, you asked me about a previous decision of the chief of the General Staff who proved some form of co-operation between the MUP and the army. I'm answering that I can't know with any degree of certainty whether such a decision in fact existed. As a matter of fact, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's clarified the answer. Thank you, Mr. Witness. During the course of your investigation or the commission's investigation, you've told us that Mr. Stevanovic was spoken to and interviewed; correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that Stevanovic confirmed that the -- he'd met Mr. Simatovic at Bajina Basta in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I do have to remind you that it was a member of the committee from the Ministry of the Interior that interviewed Mr. Stevanovic. No other members of the committee were present, and that includes me. The reason for that being a proposal made by one of the committee members from the MUP suggesting that he should interview Mr. Stevanovic on his own. The reason for that was the fact that he knew Mr. Stevanovic personally, and he believed that that might lead to better results in terms of Stevanovic agreeing to be interviewed, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me shortcut you if I can. Did Mr. Stevanovic give testimony about meeting Simatovic at camp Tara in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An Official Note was compiled during the interview by a member of the Ministry of the Interior committee. That note certainly suggests that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that Stevanovic had asked the Serbian MUP or the Serbian DB to organise some form of training for the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the note says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the training was to train specialised police to patrol the Serbian border, and that was the purpose of the training, to create specialised police to patrol the Serbian border at a time when the conflict in Bosnia threatened to spill into Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although the Official Note doesn't state that, it just might be the case given the fact that Mount Tara is right next to the border to Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Serbia's territory, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking actually at a note which -- let me shortcut this, didn't Stevanovic tell you that in 1993 he visited Simatovic at Tara?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe the witness has already testified that he did not do the interview, and he referred to the person from the Ministry of the Interior who did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which does not exclude for that other possibility. Could have said outside the context of that interview. But, Mr. Jordash, you started asking questions about what apparently is found in the Official Note, then you moved outside that, that was not entirely clear in your question. Now, the objection or at least the observation made by Mr. Groome may be an indication that you had not been perfectly clear on the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I did move from one to -- from the Official Note or -- of the interview with Stevanovic to a proofing note. We are just trying to find the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying, but perhaps it's also clear for the witness if you say, so apart from what we find in the Official Note and then you put your question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you not, Mr. Witness, speak to the Prosecution on the 7th of September, 2010, and state that Stevanovic had told you that in 1993 -- I beg your pardon. This is for the -- I take the point. I withdraw the question and I'll leave the issue at that point for now. I want to ask you about something else in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we -- do you have a hard copy of the report? I don't know if the Prosecution have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided with a hard copy by whoever has a copy available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've just sent upstairs for the hard copy that was available last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you read the relevant portion, Mr. Jordash, that might assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 24 of the report states inter alia this, and I'm referring to the JATD: "During the interview with Slobodan Miletic, the then chief of the MUP department for administrative and legal affairs, the commission discovered the information that in the Ministry of the Interior when certain decisions were being adopted, there was practice based on the identified needs and outside the current job classification to form units for certain tasks, but organisational documents for such units were often drafted only in consultation with this department. This way of drafting system-related documents which refer to JATD, was confirmed by Obrad Stevanovic, retired chief in the MUP of the Republic of Serbia who said that in his interview that in 1993 he personally used to go to the office which Franko Simatovic used Bajina Basta to offer suggestions relating to the drafting of organisational documents for the RDB special unit." Could you please explain what is meant by when certain decisions were being adopted there was practice based on the identified needs and outside the current job classification to form units for certain tasks, but organisational document for such units were often drafted only in consultation with this department. What does it mean that organisational documents were drafted only in consultation with this department?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be as precise as possible. I know full well what the report says, at least the part which the gentleman's quote refers to. It's either an interpretation problem or it's about the way the report has been presented. Mr. Miletic could never possibly say that such decisions were made bypassing him. Given his position in the Ministry of the Interior, he had no authority to take any decisions regarding the establishment of a new organisational component of the MUP or for that matter the RDB. Mr. Miletic spoke about a single technical matter. He tried to explain he was not involved in the drafting of the founding document regarding the establishment of a new organisational unit in the MUP or the RDB. After all, we did see the rules on the job classification and internal organisation awhile ago. That would have been the typical thing to do. He was, after all, head of the department for systemic and legal affairs, rather, he was discussing this in purely practical terms. Documents such as these, again I have to say in a technical sense, are sometimes drafted without any involvement on the part of the technical department, drafted by people in leading positions or indeed individuals from these units and special organisational structures, and that is all his statement comes down to. By saying that, he also explained that he was not involved in the drafting of any decision, resolution, or indeed any set of rules under any number bearing a date sometime in April 1993 unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On page 25 of the report at paragraph 2, the followed is noted: "Considering the then practice of drafting the documents such as the founding document for JATD, there are reasonable grounds to assume that it was probably done in two copies and filed in the log-book after the then interior minister, the deceased Zoran Sokolovic had signed it." Is this fair that a particular administration would form a particular unit, the documents for the founding of that unit would be compiled within that administration, as a general practice?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Once those documents had been drafted, they would then be sent to the interior minister, from the administration to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily in this case. In this case, it is uncertain who made the decision. Whoever makes a decision signs it off and puts it on file. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the documents dealing with the founding of the JATD would have been drafted within the administration dealing with the founding of that unit and then sent straight to the minister of interior, Sokolovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to reminds you that the RDB was part of the Ministry of the Interior. As the report very precisely states, the log-books from that period which the Prosecution has had a chance to inspect on several occasions contain no document under that filing number. It's not there. Based on the structure of the filing number, the committee merely drew the conclusion that the document had probably been passed by minister and then filed in the log-book of the minister's cabinet which, by the way, was destroyed during NATO's air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the paragraph goes on to say: "One copy was most probably sent to the then RDB chief Jovica Stanisic, and the other was filed in the office of the interior minister which was destroyed in the NATO bombing." Why did the commission conclude that one copy was probably sent to the RDB chief, with emphasis on the probably?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: assignment, they all confirmed that such a decision, resolution, or similar document existed. Nevertheless they all agreed that they had never set eyes on it. The committee had no choice but to reach that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the -- probably appears to suggest, tell me if I'm wrong, that it wouldn't have necessarily have been sent to Mr. Stanisic as a matter of strict protocol; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I quite accept that possibility that such an additional copy, a second copy, had not been sent to Mr. Stanisic, and that maybe it had never been sent to the RDB because according to the official log-books and records, it was not logged and filed in the RDB at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the decision to establish the JATD according to the conclusions reached by the commission may well have not been seen by Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, that's the meaning of the word "probably" isn't it, if you say that something is probable, that it's not established with such a level of certainty that we can rely on that possibility which is considered to be even probable. Possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, but I was hoping that I would be able to tease out exactly what the commission meant by that word because it may indicate a different degrees of certainty or lack of certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your question was whether it was possible that he had never seen it. That's, of course, included in that it's probable. He may never have seen it because if the probability did not -- of course doesn't say that this is what happened. Let's proceed. I just want you to be aware that if the word "probable" is used in such a report, that the Chamber doesn't take that for being a fact but just for a probability. Nothing more, nothing less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The point I'm getting at, Mr. Witness, is that it was not unusual or it was quite usual for administrations within the state security to form units within those administrations and that those units be their formation and the founding documents indicating their foundation bypass, if you like, the chief of security, chief of state security?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question with absolute certainty because at the time I was not in -- on a position where I could answer this question, but I understand your question and I can say that it's not very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What's not very likely?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not likely that an administrative organ, whether it be the MUP, the RDB, or any other state organ would make -- take decisions changing their internal organisation without the leadership of that organ, administrative organ being aware of it. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the units being formed within the administrations could and did report directly at times to the minister; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the Ministry of the Interior, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to now turn to the issue of authenticity. Did I understand your evidence correctly that you hadn't seen anything to indicate that there were fabricated documents within the records found, or I should say, stored at Lipovica?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 1D01248.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: While that's coming up, could I seek some clarification from you. Were you ever looking for documents which were not authentic when going through the records?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question, I'm not sure I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you -- how much time have you spent going through the records yourself personally? Have you read everything in the records relating to what you've sent the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read all the documents that were forwarded together with the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that within the records sent to the Prosecution, there are handwritten documents lacking any official stamp?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that within the records there are typed documents without any official stamp or other identifying indices?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you have indeed concluded yourself that there was at least one fabricated document within the records?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I had that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall being shown a document relating to a criminal complaint against a man called Vasilije Mijovic?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall telling the Prosecution that you considered that a particular document had probably been manufactured by one of the Mijovic's friends and somehow placed into the records?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall saying that to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just let me try to -- I'm very short of time. That had been manufactured by one of Mijovic's friends to help Mijovic escape criminal responsibility; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to remind me when it was that I said that to the Prosecution or when, in fact, I mention at all the name of Mijovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The 2nd or 3rd of December, 2008, in a location at the BIA offices, and it was a meeting with Mr. Groome. And the note of the meeting. Do you not recall this?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who wrote that note?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think one of the representatives of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps Your Honour, I'm desperately running out of time and I really do not have the time to conduct the cross-examination I'd want to conduct, so I'm not going to take the witness to that particular section because I have other things I have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you read it briefly to us, because one of the things I was asking myself when I listened to your questions is to what extent intellectual falsity and forgery of documents are strictly separated. I mean, I can produce a document which is not true to its contents but nevertheless not a forgery to the extent that I produce it myself and I do not hide that I'm the one who produces it. Although I may be lying in producing such a document. That's one of the question that came to my mind. But since I do not know what is in the note, neither do I exactly know what document you are referring at, it's questions on my mind, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The note states: "The meeting next dealt with order 33/95 which had been provided for review during the Groome-Soldal mission in October. This order had been part of a criminal case file against Vasilije Mijovic as a member of the Serbian MUP in relation to a traffic accident he had caused in 1995. The BIA officials stated that they did not consider this to be a genuine document issued by the JATD, in view of the signature and stamp (stating Serbian Republic of Krajina) but that it had probably been manufactured by one of Mijovic's friends to help Mijovic escape criminal responsibility."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I understand then that it's considered to be authentically a part of that file but found it's way in there as a result of fraud or forgery?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To be fair to the witness, it looks as though it was said by an unidentified official rather than the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the one focused question you could ask the witness about it. Perhaps he now remembers what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you remember this discussion?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this discussion but I can explain what it is that you are getting at, if you allow me, I can be very precise. It was like this, a certain individual actually sued the Republic of Serbia for damages caused by an individual called Vlastimir Mijovic claiming that the state of Serbia is responsible for the damage incurred in this traffic accident because Mr. Mijovic, according to what was alleged, was at the time a member of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. The attorney who was in charge of protecting the interests of the Republic of Serbia, he is referred to as the public attorney in Serbia, he replied to this claim by the citizen. The BIA at the time sought information on whether Mr. Mijovic was in fact a member of the Ministry of the Interior, or rather, the RDB. In one such case where a certain individual was a leader of a unit, the answer was that Mr. Mijovic was not a member of JSO, and that answer was signed by the commander. However, after awhile, a totally different individual submitted or sued the same individual or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Witness, I'm going to have to cut you off because I'm running out of time. Do you remember -- I'm sorry, I don't mean to be rude, but do you recall that it was the view of some unidentified BIA official at the meeting that a document, the document I've just referred to, had been manufactured and placed into the records?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just so the record is clear, the note doesn't indicate, I'm trying to verify now, where this actual document came from. It's not clear, it may very well have come from a court case file and not from the archives, but I'm still investigating this, so I ask Mr. Jordash to keep that in mind as he phrases his questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I can answer this question. No BIA member who took part in these talks could have said anything to that effect, because simply put, it's not true. The agency sought and has different answers from that same institution, the JSO, regarding that same question, and the agency was not trying to conceal that it had two opposing documents which actually exclude one another, but this does not mean that someone within the agency actually falsified the document because this -- the agency itself actually showed and presented both of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have page 3 of the document on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What is that a photograph of, please?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph depicts and shows the state in which we found the personnel files for former JSO members after the take-over had been done where it had been taken over by the MUP in April 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How did the document end up in this rather disheveled state?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to put that question to the person who was responsible for safeguarding these documents because after we handed over the documents, my responsibility ended with that. There was no other responsibility on our part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you are not able to provide the Court with evidence concerning how the documents were carried to this room and placed in the manner in which we see them?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot say anything about that. You probably know that the Ministry of the Interior and the BIA in 2002 were two separate state organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you cannot give evidence concerning how many people were involved in transporting those documents and placing them in the manner in which we see them?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about it because I had no part in this and I had no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Or who had access to the documents before they were put into the room in that way?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who had access to them but working as a member of this commission, I could see that the Office of the Prosecutor and its investigators had at least three times access to these documents and we did not have -- as for our part, we did not have access to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if the point you'd like to make is that a documentation, the status we see it on the picture, creates great risks of unreliability, then that point is clear; not to say that it was unreliable, but at least that the way in which it was organised certainly favoured rather than disfavoured that documents would either be lost or added easily or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Witness, you were asked to conduct an investigation involving the -- a unit called the JPN; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was one the tasks set before the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct, is this fair, that having conducted your investigation, the conclusion reached was that the JATD was the first ad hoc unit formed by the DB during the 1991 to 1996?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that conclusion can be reached, but I would confine the time-frame to April 1993 through April 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in relation to 1991 to 1993, there was nothing in the records to indicate the DB had a unit as such akin to the JATD, or the later JSO?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agency does not have any document pointing in that direction, nor do I have any knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will stop there because I'm running out of time, I would ideally have liked to take the witness through some of the documents but I want to save some time for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd say some of the documents which might raise doubt just to the authenticity, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, would it be an idea that you provide those documents to the witness, ask him to look at it, and see whether after the break there's anything where apparently you earlier said that there was no -- that he had nothing that he considered to be an indication of lack of authenticity, whether that still would be his view if he looked at those documents. Is that -- I'm not trying to take over, but would that be a solution and would that at least enlarge the possibilities in putting questions to the witness, perhaps by briefly saying did you look at this, did you look at that, did you look at that? I'm just wondering whether that would assist you in eliciting as much information from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'd be certainly happy to try, Your Honour. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it then be a good idea that you provide the witness with copies of, I take it, the copies in the original copies, and that he is invited during the break to carefully look at them again and whether he sees anything which looks strange to him or which would be a clue for the purpose of questioning the authenticity. If that's something which would assist you, then that might --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I certainly will do that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm looking at -- yes, Mr. Groome, I take it that you would like it to know what documents will be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, that, Your Honour, and I have another matter that I must raise before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the break. In the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think it will be no harm to raise it in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, may I just tender the picture of the store as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't know whether this is -- whether you consider this to be state secret or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't. We'll hear later from other interested parties whether they would consider it to be state secret. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at 2.17 today the Simatovic Defence notified of us of 29 documents that they would use in cross-examination of this witness, the totals 1.600 pages. This notice is, according to the practices and agreements between the parties, is six days late. I think fairness requires that over the break that the Simatovic Defence be directed to indicate to the Chamber which among these 1.600 pages they intend to put before the witness so we can prepare ourselves. We are still printing them out, but as they arrive here in the courtroom I hardly will have the time to be able to read so many pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll see also how they are going to be used in order to see what the real problem is. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first I'd like to say that our notice was sent when it was because we had a problem with the documents that had been disclosed tardily. And we discussed this last week. That's number one. Number two, most of those documents are not necessary. These are notes on questioning and they have to do with the questioning of Obrad Stevanovic before this Tribunal. Most of these documents relate to that, the questioning of Mr. Stevanovic in the Milosevic case, so I don't think that would pose a major problem to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's see how it turns out to be. Too often it happens that we have major problems and sometimes forget that the proof of the pudding is in the eating and not in the discussion before even tasting the pudding. We'll have a break and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we resume, the Chamber received an informal message about submissions to be made by the Republic of Serbia in relation to the closed -- the protective measures for this session. The Chamber will phrase very specific questions in this context and will invite you to make written submissions on the matter, and as long that we have not received that, of course everything will stay as it is at this moment for the time being. Then, of course the parties will have an opportunity to respond to that, and then finally we'll decide on the matter. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you have the opportunity to look at those documents?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have quickly P473 on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is there anything about this document which indicates to you that it is authentic or not authentic?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't notice anything about this document that would challenge its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise -- well, have a look there at the signature which purports to be Mr. Stanisic, and just keep that in your mind for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And may I then have on the screen P406. I don't know go we can keep the B/C/S version of the present document on the screen and pull up a B/C/S document of P406 so we can look at signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the document you were seeking?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking for, Your Honour, ERN 0641-4640. That's the one, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was wondering, Mr. Witness, whether you are able to say anything about the signature of Mr. Stanisic, whether you would recognise one or both or neither as Mr. Stanisic's signature as you've seen on other documents?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise for not being able to answer this question with certainty. I am not qualified to give a forensic opinion on signatures. At the first glance when I compare the two documents, it seems quite unequivocal that the signatures are identical, if nothing, it's about the physical length of the two signatures. I yet again have to apologise. I never worked directly with Mr. Stanisic, therefore, I never had an opportunity to really deliberately study his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you a few questions on this. Did you pay attention to it when you looked at the document on the left of your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever considered to ask for an expert opinion about -- in comparing the signatures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anyone else, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would suggest that the two signatures there look quite different. You don't agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't suppose my answer would be relevant. I can agree that there is a difference between the two signatures, the way in which the signatures were placed. However, I can't assert that these are two signatures by two different persons, whether the two documents were signed by different hands belonging to different people in fact. I cannot assert anything either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the point which you apparently want to make is clear to us, whatever our conclusions would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, if we could look at the document on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we could have the English version of that now on right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It purports to be an operative cheque for the special unit of the Serbian MUP. Sorry, let me put that again. It purports to be a request for an operative cheque for the special unit of the Serbian MUP on the 20th of February, 1992. Would you agree from what you've told us that the evidence you looked at did not suggest there was a special unit of the Serbian MUP, certainly not the special unit of the DB in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know that there was an RDB special unit prior to April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what is it -- is there anything which would identify this document as authentic rather than there being nothing on it which suggests it's not authentic? What is it about the document which suggests it is authentic?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the upper left corner there is a header and filing number. The filing number was registered as such in the log-book, 02 official secret, strictly confidential, the number, and the date when the document was logged. I suppose if one goes back to the log-book, the strictly confidential RDB from 1992, and inspects it, as far as I can tell the date is the 28th of August, one could to a certain extent establish whether a document like this ever existed or was logged. Nevertheless, this would still not constitute absolute certainty in terms of the document really being signed by the person whose signature is displayed on the face of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where is the log-book that might assist?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose in the security and information agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you think it might be available? Have the Prosecution asked you for that log-book?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The OTP have had a chance to inspect these log-books of the RDB. I suppose they looked into 1992 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh. Okay. So we'll leave it at that. The Prosecution have looked at the log-book. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll leave it there, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the next step to see whether it could be verified, because this apparently is a contested document and it might bring us one step further to a solution of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I was leaving it as if the Prosecution have the log-book, then they'll produce it as corroboration of their case in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll investigate to verify, but my recollection is that the Prosecution does not have the log-book. They were offered the log-book to look and the Prosecution then selected documents or made requests of documents in the log-book that appeared to be of interest for this case and that's how we obtained these documents. I don't know that we were ever given by Serbia a copy of the log-book, but I think the witness may -- his recollection on this matter might be more accurate than mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see what happens and whether if the parties do not pursue the matter, whether the Chamber would like to have a look at what on this date is entered into the log-book. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll leave it at that. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness JF-095, you'll be now cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic, but before I give that opportunity, I'd first like to invite Madam Registrar to assign a number to the photograph of the disorganised archive we saw before the break. That was 1D1248. Madam Registrar, that receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D1248.1 under which number is now photograph uploaded will be Exhibit D114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence provisionally under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness. First of all, I would like to ask you to tell me in a few words about your professional background, your education, and your career?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Between 1990 and 1999 can you tell us where you worked at that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness. If you know, please, I'd just like to make this even more concise, if possible. The other two members of the committee from the BIA, do you know anything about their careers between 1990 and 1999 specifically, the commission members?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question with any certainty or precision. I believe there was this gentleman who joined the service much later after me. As for the lady involved, I believe she had also been a member of the service for a considerable amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, what about the commission reports which is the subject of our exchange here today. The annexes contain some of the general documents that I believe were used before the drafting of the report. Can you tell us whether in addition to all these documents listed in the annex there were other general documents providing guide-lines for the work of the state security service and were those also used for the purposes of drafting the present report?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general documents that are in the annexes were not used for the drafting of this report. They were listed because one of the assistance points was about the delivery of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what general enactments were actually used when the report was drafted?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which general enactments do you have in mind, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I mean, enactments regulating the work of the state security service?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be very specific. The commission was established pursuant to a decision of the government of the Republic of Serbia dated November 2008. The decision detailed the commission's tasks. The fact was the commission did not have the authority to prosecute, therefore no general enactments were required for its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, if we look at the commission's conclusions, specifically page 29 of the report in the Serbian, as I'm sure you know it reads: "In accordance with the generally accepted standards of the RDB under the norms applying then it had the authority to enlist the assistance of a person that would then help with their work." And it goes on to talk about documents and so on and so forth. My question then as now, what would be the norms you invoked while drafting this part of your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the norms in place at the time, this would have been the rules governing the work of the state security service. Further, rules on the methods and means used in the work of the state security service that applied at the time and in part also the law on the basics of the state security service system. Now it would be the law on the legislative information agency -- security information agency and the instructions governing its work. There are some special measures and steps provided for. The RDB and the BIA, in order to perform work from their purview, has the power of enlisting the external persons to help them with it, to help them achieve their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness. There is a correction perhaps that I'd like to make and perhaps I just misunderstood what you said earlier on. At some point today earlier on you mentioned April 1993 through April 1996 while describing the time-period throughout which this unit existed that was mentioned in the OTP's motion. Did I get it right, did you mean to say April or did you mean to say August since the documents that you analysed were dated August 1993? It is possible that I misunderstood what you said.

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your understanding is correct, I did say April 1993. This is an enactment that can be read as a founding document. Unless I'm mistaken, it's from August 1993. I don't have it in front of me. If I said April, then I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's the one thing that I wanted to clarify. Based on your knowledge sir, under the constitution of the Republic of Serbia adopted in 1990, were there any obligations for the state of Serbia or the state organs vis-a-vis Serbs living outside its territory?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question with any certainty. I do assume that there were certain commitments. The present constitution of the Republic of Serbia mentions certain commitments on the part of the Republic of Serbia vis-a-vis what we now call its diaspora. Would have been the case all the more so perhaps earlier on when there was still a single country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether general enactments of the MUP or the RDB defined any obligations or commitments of those organs vis-a-vis Serbs living outside the Republic of Serbia's territory?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the general enactments for the RDB, I don't suppose there was a category like that. But again, I can't say with certainty. These are issues that would require an inspection of the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'd be happy to show you a document entitled "Description of Classified Jobs."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 65 ter 2377. It's an OTP document. Page 12 and page 13. The title page first of all, followed by pages 12 and 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is the title page, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now move on to page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the bottom of the page where it says "the second administration," "the chief of the administration." So let's look at this paragraph that appears on this page, and then can we move on to the next page, the top of the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists and saves time, the Prosecution would not object to the tendering or the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only wanted to ask a few questions of the witness regarding this. I did not really intend to tender it, but there is no problem with tendering it if that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't understand Mr. Groome's observation to be an objection to further questions being put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I just had a question for you. Were you able to read these two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this is one of those enactments regulating and defining at the level of the service, in other words, the second administration, the commitments vis-a-vis the Serbs who lived outside the territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for your reference, this is on pages 10 and 11 in the English version. I see that we don't have it on the monitors yet in English. Your Honour, as my learned colleague has no objection, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D115, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D115 is admitted into evidence for the time being under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you are aware surely, and you mentioned a moment ago a document entitled "Rules of Service of the State Security Service." That document provides for the means and methods used by the service, and what I would like to inquiry about is the co-operation as one of those methods and operative means. So my question for you is this: Can collaboration or co-operation be established on the basis of one's patriotism, loyalty that to the state, et cetera? Could that be one of the basis for it?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, and that is one of the primary bases for actually establishing a collaborative relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can this collaboration also be established on the basis of some remunerative principles?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can collaboration also be established with foreign citizens on the basis of friendship or some political motives or any other basis?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can collaboration be established with a member of a foreign intelligence, a foreign army, or even a terrorist or some other organisation?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the rules of service for the state security service, among the tasks that are mentioned for operatives, one of them is tasks that are envisioned for extraordinary circumstances such as a threat of war or a state of war; correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can the service -- can the service compensate its collaborator for a task or a job done?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If the collaboration is based on the remunerative principle, does the service -- does there arise on the part of the service a certain obligation towards that collaborator?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. If the motive for co-operation that was promised to the collaborator is material remuneration, then that would have to be met.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the service have any obligations in certain circumstances vis-a-vis members of families of the collaborators, or do they have to provide some forms of special technical assistance such as legal assistance or some other assistance?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the event that the security of the collaborator is threatened or that a collaborator had lost his life in service, such a person and his family members would enjoy all the benefits that the regular employees of the service enjoy. The same is true in the event that an individual was arrested or criminal proceedings have been instituted against him, that person would be entitled to material assistance provided that the proceedings were not initiated by the service itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, before we continue, you referred as far as Serbs living outside the republic, you refer to pages 10 and 11, and I think in B/C/S 13. I only found something on e-court page 9. Could you please verify that we didn't miss anything. By the way, the numbering of pages is a bit confusing because the numbering at the bottom of the page, it restarts halfway the document. But could you, not necessarily now, but keep in the back of your mind that the Chamber would appreciate a very precise reference so that we know where to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will do that during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, first of all let me ask you, do you have the commission report before you?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 21, that's section 4. I would like to refer you to the portion where it says that the commission has obtained information that in the work of the MUP it was standard practice to employ regardless of the job classification that is in force, to employ certain individuals for certain tasks and assignments. Could you please just clarify this part which says "outside of the job classification in force." My understanding was that this part of the commission report was drafted based on the interview with Mr. Miletic, and in the note on the interview I did not actually find any place where he mentioned that this can be done outside of the job classification. First, so could you please just describe or explain why this terminology was used, perhaps I did not understand something correctly, or maybe you can just shed some light on this?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The fact is that the paragraph that you are referring to is to a certain degree contradictory because Mr. Miletic mostly discussed the manner in which the founding documents were produced, and the participation or non-participation of his unit in the production of those documents. Now, if founding documents are being produced and they affect the existing job classification, then one cannot really say that a unit may be formed outside of the job classification in force. I assume that Mr. Miletic, just as the other members of the commission, had in mind when said this that of the -- had in mind the fact that a unit referred to here is a unit that is in the process of being established. So it wasn't really envisaged in the enactment. However, once it is established and once it becomes part of the existing enactment or a whole new enactment is adopted, then such an organisational unit is not outside of the scope of the enactment in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I understood, you could find proof that the job classification had actually been put in place and that it was, in accordance with this job classification that action was taken?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we found evidence of this in one of the personnel files that was found in the Lipovica store where we found an adjusted table of jobs and posts which table was part of every rules of service, but as I already told the Prosecutor, I don't know whether it is this -- these rules of service that we have -- that we are discussing here because I can't really tell without seeing the number in the heading. Whether it is the rules of service of August 1993, I cannot really ascertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please take a look at P476.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We will have it before us this a moment and could you just tell us whether the designation that we find where reference is made to the job classification, does it correspond to the job classification as provided in the document that you mention, the handwritten document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For reference, let me say that it's P974.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. From this -- from the table we could conclude that that is the document in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Now, I have a few questions that you may find quite ordinary, but they are significant to us in view of the evidence that is already before this Trial Chamber. You marked last week for us the place where the BIA headquarters is in Banjica. Now, do you know how long the BIA and its predecessor, the SDB, were actually housed in that -- on those premises?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as -- if I'm not mistaken, the seat of the service of the SDB or the BIA was there as of the spring of 2004, but it is possible that I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the headquarters of the SDB was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was in Kneza Milosa Street in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know what was in Banjica on the premises where the BIA is today? What was on those premises in the period between 1991 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was the security institute of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us this security institute, was this a federal institution which then later was transformed into a republican Serbian institution or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a federal institution, a federal body or agency, which as far as I know and as you can deduce from its name was a research facility actually. And also an educational facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few questions about Obrad Stevanovic. Could you tell us, please, who made the decision to interview this person?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was taken by the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You have the commission report before you, part of which are also the notes, official minutes on your work. Now, could you please tell us whether -- I've tried to find some of these documents in the attachments but I couldn't really find it?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely at the time, but I think you're referring to one of the first sessions of the commission, maybe not the constitutive session but the following one. And I'm not sure that such a decision is actually mentioned in the law?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the official notes I did not find any mention of Mr. Stevanovic's interview in that decision, but I did find a decision relating to all the other individuals. This was adopted on the second, during the second meeting; for instance, at the second meeting it was

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was an omission that occurred during the drafting of the report. We did discuss interviewing this individual at the commission, and as I've already said the member of the commission from the Republic of Serbia MUP actually initiated and proposed that he himself conduct the interview with this person and that was accepted by the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just tell us whose proposal was this to interview this individual?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a proposal by the member of the commission from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did only one individual conduct this interview with Obrad Stevanovic when the interviews with all the other individuals were conducted by all three members or at least two members of the commission?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already answered that question, but let me repeat: The proposal that was put forth by this member of the Ministry of the Interior was that he should conduct this interview on his own. He said that he knew the person, that he knew this man personally and that this would yield better results and that Mr. Stevanovic would not have any -- he would not oppose and show any kind of negative response to the questions posed by the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now about the co-operation between the BIA and the OTP. What about the Prosecutor in this case, did they at any point ask you to help them get in touch with anyone from the BIA, be it an active employee or retired?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that has been the case on one or two occasions, and the people in question were active employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you respond to that request?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm in no position to make such decisions. Nevertheless, when the right person was addressed, the person with the power to make such decisions, the response that came back was a positive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Mr. Groome phoned you so that you could help him identify the right persons to talk to?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never spoke to Mr. Groome on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My apologies, I misinterpreted something. At any rate, did Mr. Groome ask you when you met to later phone you and for you to help him identify some people to talk to, was that the situation?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Groome never requested a conversation with me in terms of identifying people. In the request for assistance he did mention something about a videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I'm done with my questioning of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Jordash, one question came to my mind you asked a few questions in relation to the documents and authenticity. Did you give him more than the ones you dealt with in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I gave him -- yes, we gave him another disputed document allegedly signed by Mr. Stanisic, but I was content to leave it because the answers would be applicable to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine that the answers being of a rather general nature on what -- yes, that's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, though, I would -- in light of the time, and I think we would finish both witnesses today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And one of the things I do not know yet is how much time you would need for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would need no more than 15 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Petrovic, how much would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, an hour perhaps. An hour and a quarter perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then you were rather optimistic, Mr. Jordash. I mean, well, depends on whether it's 15 minutes or 30 minutes and one hour and a quarter, one hour. Mr. Groome, as I understand now, how much time do you think you would need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have five questions, Your Honour. I think no more than five minutes or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five, six minutes. Mr. Jordash, have you negotiated the time claimed by Mr. Petrovic down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
