utterances.text: I don't think so at the moment, but I was going to request an additional five minutes with this witness to deal with some issues which I would like to deal with if at all possible. It's 10 minutes rather than five to be frank with the Court, but I would if time allows. I'd be happy to leave it until the end to see if Mr. Petrovic does indeed take that long with the next witness. I certainly will not be more than 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you'll have a couple more minutes. If you say I certainly do not need more than 30 minutes, that's of course already more pessimistic than 15 to 30 minute, but the reason why I am allowing you now to ask further questions to the witness is because asking him to remain standby and to have him enter the courtroom and going out again might take more time than -- so please be as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I have on the screen, please, 1D1274.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we turn, please, to page 23617. Let's go to 23616.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the top reads, the top paragraph reads:

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you say those words?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I can't remember every single word I've ever uttered. A lot of time has gone by. I can hardly be expected to confirm every single word that is recorded here as truly authentic. I am not prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would it be your view having conducted or being part of this investigation that there may be people on the payment lists that did not exist?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can neither confirm nor deny something like that. The simple truth is I don't know these people, I don't know who they are, I don't know what their jobs were. I've never met a single person from that list. Anyway, that was not the job of my commission and it wasn't in the job description of the Security and Information Agency either. I'm not an investigator and I'm not with the OTP. It is not my place here to defend or accuse anyone. I'm here to be a fact witness. I'm here to tell you about the work of the commission of which I happened to be a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: One more point if I may, then I'm finished. If we look further down on the same page it's recorded that you made the following comment in relation to your assistance to the Prosecution:

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were surprised that these payment lists had not been destroyed in accordance with the normal procedure? Was that what you were telling the Prosecution in part on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To me that was a great surprise. Had the rules been complied with such as rules regulating how those documents were dealt with, the regular procedure would have dictated that those documents be destroyed over ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So that would -- according to the regular procedure would have entitled Mr. Stanisic as the chief of the service to destroy the documents if he had so chosen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely correct. This is not a discretionary right of the head of the RDB. There are some bylaws regulating procedures relating to documents including the destruction of documents. Here we are dealing with a document category that is normally kept for up to five years. Nevertheless, the final decision on destroying such documents is taken by the head of the RDB which would now translate into the agency director.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one follow-up question in relation to what Mr. Jordash asked you, Witness JF-095. Mr. Jordash read to you what is written down as being your response to an observation made by the OTP that while no members of Arkan's Tigers were found on the lists, you said you didn't remember exactly what you said, that was in the report of June 2008. If I would ask you that same question today, would your answer be similar or would it be different, and I -- what is written down as your answer at the time was that you had claimed that your normal circumstances that it would have been impossible that people like that would be paid DSA from the DB or the BIA but that the circumstances were not normal. Would you give a similar answer if I would put that same question to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my answer would be very similar. Nevertheless, I do owe you an explanation as to why circumstances were unusual. If the territorial integrity and the very sovereignty of a state is in jeopardy, then I suppose you will agree with me that these are unusual circumstances, including any threat to the constitutional order, and defending a constitutional order is a primary task for a service such as the RDB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you added to your answer that it could have been an abuse of public money as well and that those persons did not exist. Would you still add that to the answer you just gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The probability that that is the case is low or at least lower than the contrary. Of course there is a possibility that funds were embezzled. There is always the possibility when we are talking about public administration bodies and that applies at all times and not just in extraordinary circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness JF-095, it would have saved sometime if when asked by Mr. Jordash you would have added to the response that you do not remember exactly what you said at the time, that your answer would still be the same. And perhaps have given the same explanations as you just gave to me. I have -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: JF-095, could I first deal with the last matter that Mr. Jordash raised with you with respect to document that you produced or your agency produced to the OTP that in your view, had ordinary procedures been followed, would have been destroyed five years after their creation. Now, my question to you with respect to these documents is the following: Does the fact that they were still in existence is a more -- what is the probable explanation of the fact that they are still in existence?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most probable explanation for their existence would be lack of care, lack of professionalism, and negligence on the part of whoever was in charge of those documents, which is not to say that there might not be another reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say negligence, do you mean that they were overlooked, they weren't destroyed at the time that they were, according to the rules, intended to be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the location where BIA currently stands, when did that building come under the control of the state of Serbia and leave the control of the former Yugoslavia, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that was the case with the former federal state and its break-up, possibly 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to questions Mr. Jordash asked you with respect to signatures, I want to ask you the following question: Can the chief of the state security service, does he have the right to or the authority to delegate -- I am sorry, let me start the question again. Does the chief of the state security service have the ability to delegate the authority to sign documents on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Director of the security information agency does have that power. He has the power to authorise another person, the deputy or another authorised person to sign document on his behalf. As for the period of the RDB, I'm unable to answer that question with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jordash showed you a photograph of the container in Lipovica, and my question to you is: Are the other archives of the BIA in a similar state of disorganisation?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correction, that was not the archive of the BIA, that was the archive of the Ministry of the Interior and its special units. The archive of the BIA is definitely not in that kind of condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Petrovic with respect to D115 now in evidence, he spoke to you at length about different types of collaboration both with people within Serbia and also with friends and people who received remuneration outside the country. My question is the following: Collaboration is a somewhat vague word, can such collaboration include the commission of international crimes such as persecution, murder, forcible deportation as crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: JF-095 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume you already know what my answer would be. No service in the world, no system anywhere would you find a thing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Witness JF-095, first of all, have the questions put by Mr. Groome triggered any need for further questions? If not, I think it would be desirable if witness JF-095 would remain standby, there may be unforeseen developments in the cross-examination of the next witness. Witness JF-095, would you be willing to remain standby until 7.00 or shortly after 7.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I hope and expect that we don't have to rely on your further presence, so therefore, in case we would not see each other later today, I already would like to thank you on behalf of the Chamber for coming to The Hague and having answered -- I should say coming to The Hague twice and having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I hope that you have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at 10 minutes to 6.00. And the parties are invited to see whether there's any way of concluding their cross-examination in the 70 minutes then remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness JF-094. I'll repeat my words. Good afternoon, Witness JF-094.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. And good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness JF-094, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given last week Friday at the beginning of your testimony. No, it wasn't the Friday --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at the beginning of your testimony, even if it was not on Friday. You'll now be cross-examined. Mr. Petrovic, you'll be the first one? You will now first be cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On Wednesday you mentioned that the establishment of the commission and the production of the report was of national interest, as you put it. What is the national interest of this commission or this commission's work as you see it?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commission was established in order to respond to an RFA from the Tribunal which earlier on were -- it was impossible to provide. Some of the documents had already been provided pursuant to some other RFAs, but if you're asking me about whether I consider that this commission was of national interest and why, my understanding of it was, and as far as I could see the understanding of the other members of the commission as well, was because we put the co-operation with the Tribunal as one of the priorities. So our job was to determine where the documents which were sought by the Tribunal could be found or if they couldn't, to establish that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please just slow down a bit so that -- to make sure that the transcript is complete.

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, first of all, tell us, please, what was the reaction of the Tribunal's Office of the Prosecutor to the commission's report?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What would be the repercussions had these -- had this job not been done in a proper way, in other words, in a way that would satisfy the expectations of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I can only guess, I assume that that would affect the confidence that the Tribunal had in the work of Republic of Serbia organs and our honest wish and desire to really respond to the Tribunal's requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether after the report was submitted, the commission report, a member of which you were, do you know whether the Tribunal produced any report or statement of some sort that touched upon, among other things, the commission report, the report that you yourself participated in producing?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know about that, but I do have to mention something here. Right after the completion of the commission's work, I was not at work anymore. I actually had -- I was ill, I was taken ill, and I did not attend any of these sessions of the commission because I had measles and the other members of the commission had not ever had measles, so it was not a good idea for me to be there. So I'm not really familiar with what was transpiring and happening at the very last portions -- the last phases of the commission's work because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first five questions and I waited until after the fifth that you put to the witness do not assist the Chamber in any way. We do not see the relevance and I checked in the beginning with my colleagues. If there's a relevance, please in your next question make clear what that is. I can imagine that you are heading for whether the report was influenced in order to please the OTP, whatever, but then please ask the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that will become clearer at the end of my examination, I hope so, and if not, I apologise, and I will no longer insist on these questions if you feel they are not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned you did not attend the last several meetings of the commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's exactly what I was trying to point out. I understand English language and I see from the transcript that there was something that was omitted. I said that I was -- I did actually attend the meetings and I was there until the very end of the commission's work because of the -- although I was ill, but the other members of the commission had already been immune to that particular disease, so I did participate in the work of the commission, however, in the later phase when the report was actually drafted, I wasn't there. Whether there was some reaction and what the reaction was of the Tribunal's, that's why I wouldn't know how to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell me, please, who was it of the commission members who proposed that an interview be conducted with Obrad Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you put such a proposal forward?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply because I was of the opinion that Mr. Obrad Stevanovic had information that was relevant to the commission's work. Now, in view of the fact that I myself never participated -- never was an actor in those events, in the events of 1991 and 1992 because I wasn't even employed then with the service I only

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: documents were relevant or not to the establishment of the commission that were sought. And also the members of the commission who are from the BIA did not know who it was who could help with the search for the documents that had to do with the JPO, so I could say that we were actually just trying to suss out information working blind as it were. So we were trying to find people who could have some information about the events that the commission was working on. And this was in early 1990. This person was at a high position in the Serbian MUP and he was, among other things, in charge of the work of Special Police Units. So it was my proposal that he should be interviewed because I felt that he might be a person who could provide some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your evidence correctly a few days ago, you said that you interviewed this person and that then the other members of the commission were supposed to assess whether they should interview him too?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please just be as brief as possible in your answers because we don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the point. Our intention was first of all to have a preliminary interview with some individuals who might possess some information and maybe not, so I interviewed Mr. Stevanovic in his home. We discussed matters that related to the RFA itself, and I said what I said and you can see that in the material that we provided. And it was assessed by the commission that Mr. Obrad Stevanovic did not know anything that might be relevant to the commission's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to know. Now, you interviewed him in his home. Did you record that interview?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any notes? Did you take any notes during the interview?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that this was a brief interview, I did not really make any notes. I just jotted down in my notebook when the interview was conducted really as a reminder for later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, so the substance of this Official Note is what you could actually recall when you returned to your office and then dictated or whatever, typed the report; correct?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So how many days later did you actually produce this note of this interview?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps four to five days later. I can check the exact date because I have that written down, but also in the meantime we had had a meeting, the commission had had a meeting and they were briefed on the contents of Mr. Stevanovic's statement during this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your interview of Mr. Stevanovic, did you have any powers that under the Law on Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the commission did not have any such authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you warn Mr. Stevanovic that it was -- that he was obliged to tell the truth during the interview?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told him what the purpose of the interview was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But you did not issue any warnings in terms of the Law on Criminal Procedure?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would there be any legal consequences for Stevanovic if he provided some false information during that interview?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm a bit surprised by your answer in view of the fact that you are an experienced police officer, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is bearing in mind that this was an informal conversation, this was not an official interview either in the pre-trial proceedings or in criminal proceedings. This was just a preliminary interview so that I cannot really see how Mr. Stevanovic could be held liable for anything unless he would say things that would be damaging to state interests and so on. In view of the fact that this was a preliminary interview, personally I don't believe that would be the case, so I can't really answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During that interview did Stevanovic tell you that during the war from 1991 to 1995 every unit wanted to be called the Red Berets and that if they had red berets as part of their uniform and equipment that they would actually call themselves Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't say it in so many words, however, he did mention as we later --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please focus on my question. Just answer with a yes or no. If it's no, then it's no.

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall that it was said in so many words. He did say that there were different kinds of units that were not necessarily units that had anything to do with any legal authorities, either official or not. So we didn't really discuss any units that had no ties with the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, or let's call them regular units because the documents here and the request that was sought was about units or relating to units that had to do with the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Stevanovic tell you that he actually attended the establishment of JSO in 1996?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, he said in view of the fact that the request was to do with the JATD and the JPN units, we only discussed his co-operation with the JATD because that had to do with Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the note, Official Note or notes actually of this interview, it says, and you probably have it before you, would you please take a look at page 2 of that interview with Mr. Stevanovic. Here it says that he made proposals in respect of various organisational enactments and that that was the first time that he had heard the term "JATD"?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for my answer [as interpreted]. In other words, that in 1993 it was the first time that he heard this term JATD? That's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding, that he had heard of JATD for the first time in 1993 and that that was one of the names that was used for a new unit that had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, please focus on my question. So this is what he said?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, did Obrad Stevanovic say what he said to you the same thing that he said under oath here before this Trial Chamber, and that is that he was not aware that there had been any predecessor unit to JSO from 1991? Did he say that, that he did not know that there was a unit in 1991 that was -- that preceded the JSO?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that. He only talked about JATD, he said when that was established and when he had heard about it. He heard about it in a conversation with Mr. Simatovic and it was one of the proposals that were put forth to call it that. He didn't even mention the JPN at the time because that was one of the accepted -- it was one of the alternative names that were proposed as possible name for that unit that was being established at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Petrovic is going to cite the transcripts, I'd appreciate a reference so that I can find it among the hundreds of pages of the -- of Mr. Stevanovic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 40106, 40106, and we can find that in 2D229. That is a note from the interview with Stevanovic on the 27th of May, 2005. In response to Jeffery Nice's question whether the predecessor to JSO was established in 1991, he said that he didn't know and he repeated the same thing on page 40524.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, witness, do you know that Stevanovic testified in this court for 13 days, five of which he was questioned by Jeffery Nice, not exclusively about but for the most part about the JATD and JPN and that he never said, as far as I could see because I looked through all those pages, he never mentioned that anywhere? In other words, he did not know anything about the JSO and its establishment before 1996?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that but what he said here is not really contradictory to that. He didn't say that the JATD was established at the time. He said that that was one of the names that were put forth to use that name for a unit that was being established and he learned this from a conversation with Mr. Simatovic, but he wasn't even sure that that was what it was called. He said that it was one of the names that were bandied about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm questioning you -- I'm telling you that Mr. Obrad Stevanovic who testified here before this court and never mentioned that he had any knowledge about JATD, JPN or anything else that could be a predecessor to JSO?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understood what you've said and I'm repeating for the third time what I recall. This was the substance of our conversation and this is how I noted it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, how can I fairly assess whether there's no mention of the JATD without reading the entire transcript or doing word searches on it? I mean, there are hundreds of pages here. I'd ask that if Mr. Petrovic is going to use the transcript that he put specific portions to the witness so the witness can fairly answer and I can fairly examine the transcript to see if it's in proper context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the witness hasn't read it, the Chamber hasn't read it, it's not in evidence. Whatever way you summarise it, it's unverifiable for us. Now, the witness gave an answer to your question not casting any doubt on whether you are correct or not, so therefore there was no reason to intervene, but it -- it doesn't really help to seek a witness who has not read the transcript to tell us what is in there, and the Chamber also we can't verify it, so that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Chamber is in a position to check which might unfortunately be quite difficult since this is some comprehensive material, but the Chamber is in a position to check what is there and what's not. I am just trying to get the witness to tell me whether he told him any of the things that he said in court under oath. If not, very well, I have nothing further to pursue or indeed to imply. Did he hear anything like that or not, if not I'll just move on. That's the substance I've been trying to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. How do you consider us to verify the testimony of Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's complicated indeed. I could move for that to be under Rule 89 as part of this trial's evidence; however, that does strike me as a rational idea. As for a rational way to do this, I'll try to think of something. I don't think it would make any sense to research this, least of all to have 5.000 pages of the transcript become part of this case's evidence. That's why I was focusing on certain portions of the transcript which are easy enough to track down. If the OTP can find something else, they could as well present this something else, whatever they come across, and then we can deal with it in that way by dealing with certain portions of the transcript, selected ones that we might then show the witness and indeed the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I don't think you would wish us to start reading transcripts of all other cases and then to be unknown to the parties be influenced by that. I take it that that's the last thing you want to achieve, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. Thank you. The witness is here now, I can read the relevant transcript pages so we have several hundreds of pages and we can pair that back to a total of five or six which makes our task a lot easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Stevanovic tell that you he was a chief of the MUP staff of Serbia in February and March 1993 at the Bosnian Serbian border in Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just touched upon Bajina Basta, generally speaking, because he says that he was there with the Uzice detachment at the time protecting the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina because of the problems that were happening and the attacks from Bosnian territory on Serbia. There was firing there and several persons died, at least that's what he said, that's why the PJP was there, in order to prevent any incursions, and also to assist the army because many people were running away from that territory across the Drina into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But he didn't tell you that he was the chief of a staff that was actually in the area, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the note says is what he told me. He says he was involved. In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is 40241. Did he tell you that he was in charge of a staff based in Bajina Basta in control of combat operations in terms of protecting the Republic of Serbia in that region which involved the engagement of units in BH territory? Did he say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, he told me he was involved with the PJP protecting the borders of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is 40236. Do you know anything about General Stevanovic's background, educational background?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with his file. I just know that Mr. Stevanovic was working at the police academy as a professor of police tactics. I also know, although this would boil down to hearsay, something I heard about General Stevanovic as a high ranking officer, that he had received a certain degree of military education which means that at one point or another he was probably trained at the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he completed the military academy programme which takes four year, he was from the MUP but he completed the military academy, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard from my colleagues but I did not look at his file.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Back to a particular portion of your testimony. On Wednesday where you say Mr. Simatovic had some experience with combat actions and training special units. You said that on 7062. The one thing that I would like to ask you to do now is to tell me whether you know this: Mr. Simatovic, what was his background in terms of formal education and training?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. Besides, I don't remember saying that Mr. Simatovic had any combat experience. It was according to Mr. Stevanovic's words. He had heard that Mr. Simatovic was in charge of a group of people at the Tara camp who passed themselves off as people with combat experience and people who could help train the PJP, and one of the PJP's tasks in war time was something closely related to combat assignments and also disrupting public law and order and preventing that from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [English] "On the other hand, Mr. [Indiscernible] had experiences related to combat actions or to the training for special units..." [Interpretation] Now, that is not what General Stevanovic told you, is it?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, if I remember well, if those were the words, I tried to paraphrase what Mr. Simatovic had said. It wasn't me saying something that I actually knew. I never even met. I hadn't met Mr. Simatovic until after 2006 when I ended up in my present job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Stevanovic ever tell you that Simatovic had experience related to combat actions, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that Simatovic was this charge of a camp where there were people who, as he said, passed themselves off as people with combat experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You have the note right in front of you. Could you please try to track that down. You say he told you that Simatovic was in charge of a camp. Where exactly does the note reflect that?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The note says that he was for the first time in touch with Vasinovic [phoen], Simatovic, and others who had this camp at Tara, and in his words they were passing themselves off or advertising themselves. That's at page 1 if you look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not sure you understand me correctly. Where does it say that Obrad Stevanovic told you that Simatovic had experience related to combat actions? Where does your notebook say that?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not actually know that I said that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7062, Your Honours. But we might as well move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You go on to say this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see now what -- what I read on 7062 is that during the interview he would have said that Mr. Simatovic would have had some experience, some combat experience; however, that Mr. Obradovic [sic] would have another experience but that there was a sort of exchange of information between the two of them. That's what I read in the transcript and in the Official Note, I read "and according to him they advertised themselves as a special unit composed of people with combat experience." That's not exactly the same but comes close to it, isn't it? I'm just trying to understand what the issue is in order to fully grab what you want to establish and not miss the point you are intending to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my understanding they were advertising themselves as a special unit or passing themselves off as a special unit comprising people with experience of war. This can by no means mean that Simatovic had experience in combat actions. In my humble opinion, these are two entirely different matters. I will leave it to the Chamber to judge and assess but that is certainly my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say advertising themselves would be the unit and not in any way relate to Mr. Simatovic himself, is that how I have to understand your understanding of what I read in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the context is that some people were advertising themselves or passing themselves off as a unit. In the very next paragraph you say mand that's what Stevanovic says, there was no unit at all, not in a textbook sense of the word. This is someone advertising themselves as something that is no unit at all in the textbook sense of the term. Therefore, there is quite a number of differences there in relation to the sentence that the witness now denied ever uttering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand the testimony of the witness to be not that he said that Mr. Simatovic had combat experience but that it was Mr. Simatovic who would have told that to Mr. Stevanovic; is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is not my understanding, and I believe that transpires clearly from this. The witness keeps recounting his conversation with Stevanovic. He is recounting what Stevanovic is telling him. Stevanovic is telling him, at least as the present witness claims, that Stevanovic told him, the witness, that Stevanovic said that Simatovic had combat experience. That is my reading, but perhaps we should not waste any more time on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps apparently a key line is "according to him" which we find on 7062, line -- for me it's line 24. Whether that extends also to the next sentence where it reads "on the other hand, Mr. Simatovic had experiences related to combat actions." The question therefore is whether according to him still applies to the following sentence, yes or no, because in that case it would be the words of Mr. Simatovic rather than the words of Mr. Stevanovic. Let's proceed. We'll carefully analyse the texts. The only reason I'm intervening is because I really want to grab what you are actually -- what you are trying to establish so that we do not misunderstand the questions and the answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's leave the transcript aside for the moment then. Therefore, my question to you, witness, is as follows: Did Stevanovic tell you that Simatovic had experience in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to think back. I don't think I said that he had experience in combat operations. I think it might be a good idea to listen to the tape to see what was actually said. I believe that I said he had experience in the combat context of policing or police affairs. If I remember what I said a couple of days ago, that was in reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You may have said that several days ago, but my question now is let's start anew and sweep the board clean. Did Stevanovic tell that you Simatovic had experience in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevanovic told me what I wrote down, that he had heard there were people in that camp who were advertising themselves as people with combat experience. And that there had been an exchange of experience between Mr. Simatovic, at least as the policing part of this combat in war time is concerned, if that's what you prefer, while Mr. Stevanovic who had experience that would be that, but obviously --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore Stevanovic did not as a matter of fact tell you that Franko Simatovic had experience in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevanovic did not tell me that Simatovic had told him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Stevanovic tell you that Simatovic was a leader or someone in charge of that group of men at Tara?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the impression from that conversation, my impression was that he was in some way in charge of that group because he and Mr. Stevanovic were in touch about training and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That being your impression, why did you not actually write that down in your Official Note?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't strike me as important. We were talking about JATD and JPN.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. You were investigating the whereabouts of documents that might reveal what the Prosecution was after, someone tells you that another person is in charge of a certain group of men which doesn't strike you as relevant in terms of writing down and including in your Official Note?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task had to do with this and this alone. I had no criminal authority and I wasn't interested in anything else for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So why did you say that in this courtroom if weren't interested back at the time, if that is not the subject of your testimony? What led you to talk about these things now?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simple, someone asked me the question. The purpose of that interview was to see whether Mr. Stevanovic knew anything about the existence of JATD or how it came into existence. I couldn't answer these questions because obviously this is a question which stems from the work of the commission and its effort to track down documents. Nevertheless, if you ask me, even now as far as these documents are concerned, I don't see an immediate link.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you said that you had the impression, that you gained an impression during that interview that Simatovic was in some way in charge of that group of men, nevertheless Stevanovic never explicitly stated that. What we were talking about is your impression; right?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This was not a unit. He but -- said several times that this was a group of men, and he was consulted on how documents should be compiled for a unit to be established. Again, he in turn was under the impression that this was not a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of what the OTP's request was in relation to, which trial? Did you know the trial documents were required for, was that within your purview or not?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should go back to the original request but normally a request would state a case number and a trial. Prosecutor versus so and so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. What did Stevanovic tell you about Vaso Mijovic?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He simply dropped his name and that was it and that's what I wrote down. He said there was this group of men over there including Franko Simatovic, Vaso Mijovic, and others and that was all. The only time the name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he had asked Franko Simatovic to put him in touch with Vaso Mijovic?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, this was the only occasion where he mentioned the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 40263, of your evidence in Milosevic, Obrad Stevanovic said: [English] "Vasilije Mijovic is somebody I know. For awhile he worked at the training camp for the training of Special Police Units at Mount Tara, and Franko Simatovic found him at my request." [Interpretation] Did Obrad Stevanovic say to you that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, had asked the state security service to assist Obrad Stevanovic in identifying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel repeat what -- identifying what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part, had asked the state security service to assist Obrad Stevanovic in identifying, and the interpreters asked in identifying what.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Obrad Stevanovic tell you that Radovan Stojicic had asked via the state security service for assistance to him, Obrad Stevanovic, in order to find or identify instructors? Did he say that to you, Obrad Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only said that there was a need to train PJP, something to that effect, and as these people as was already mentioned were at the Tara camp and they had combat experience, a certain number of PJP members were sent to the Tara camp regardless of how that came about. I know what you want to ask me, I'm just telling you he didn't tell me how it was, but how the whole thing actually ended and how that would appear to look from today's perspective, I can tell you about that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: JF-094, could you please try to keep your answers very much focused on what is asked. Would you carefully look at Mr. Petrovic. If Mr. Petrovic with one or two words rather than starting speaking whole sentences, Mr. Petrovic, because the interpreters will not be able to follow that, but if Mr. Petrovic will interrupt you because you are going beyond what they are asking you, carefully look at him and with one or two words he will invite you to stop continuing your answer. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So your response -- your reply to my earlier question is no?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is we didn't go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, no?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall the whole question, probably so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you that Vasilije Mijovic had never been a member of the state security service of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat what I've already said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, just say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Well, I just want to say that anything you have to ask about Vasilije Mijovic, all I can answer is that he only mentioned him once.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel repeat the page number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the page number, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 40264. That is the transcript of June 1st, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, I have a few more questions for you about something else. Now, in one of the conversations that you had with the OTP, and there were quite a few, did you say and claim that there was not a single piece of paper that related to the PJP for the period after the 23rd of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What conversations are you referring to? I said that there was not a single paper after the 23rd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, could we see -- that's in your conversation of 13th November, 2006. Mr. Groome can check this. It's on page 23626.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: of paper is left from the time-period after 23rd of March, 1999." [Interpretation] In other words, you are saying that what the Prosecutor has written down here is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, here it says after the 23rd of March, 1999. Not before. This is one of the things that I can recall in respect of another MFA when in 2006 they had access to the entire documentation of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, just tell me, did you say this or not?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That suffices, just you didn't say that and that's enough. Thank you. Did you tell the OTP that the PJP, the Special Police Units, were under the command of the Pristina MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but I don't see how that relates to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, witness, it is on the Trial Chamber to decide whether my questions are relevant or not. I would just like you to answer my question?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I have to address the gentlemen here and see whether I'm free to discuss this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, very well, then let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you discussed the matter at any earlier stage with the OTP, then I really do not see any reason why it's -- no questions could be asked about that. So therefore, I invite you to answer the question. Yes. Mr. Ignjatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IGNJATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has a waiver for very specific topics. And he may actually be exposed to criminal responsibility if he discusses matters for which he does not have a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing he is asked is whether he discussed a certain matter with the Office of the Prosecution. And I don't think that so either he already violated any rule and then or -- I really do not see the point at this moment because the only thing Mr. Petrovic is asking is did you say this to the Office of the Prosecution. He is not asked about any matter which he considered to be secret at any earlier stage, if he told the Prosecution, if he did not tell the Prosecution, then he can just say no, and then of course one can wonder why someone wrote down that this is what the witness said during a conversation at any earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IGNJATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can agree and I can see how you see it this way. However, we issue a waiver to a witness before they appear here, the confidentiality clause --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I intervene at this point, I withdraw my question and we will no longer discuss this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question apparently is off the record. Now, Mr. Ignjatovic, from the decision of the Chamber, you may have seen that -- one second. You may have seen that the waiver is not binding upon this Tribunal and that if you should not refer to the waiver, what you could do is to say, while answering this question, this question should not be answered because state security interests are involved, and then we would hear you and hear all the state security interests involved in the absence of the parties and in the absence of the witness. The question apparently has been withdrawn so I suggest that we proceed. At the same time I'm very much concerned, Mr. Petrovic, about the time. I'm also looking at Mr. Jordash because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may. I understand your concern and after consulting my client, let me just say that we have no further questions for this witness. Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Petrovic. Witness, JF-094, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jordash, and Mr. Jordash will do his utmost best to finish his cross-examination before 7.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have on the screen, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Jordash, before I give you an opportunity. You raised your hand at an earlier stage and then I said wait for a second. Is there anything you would like to add to what has been said at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I would, and it has to do with the earlier question of Mr. Petrovic's with regarding my alleged remark that there was not a single paper relating to the PJP after the NATO campaign, but however, since the question has been withdrawn let me just say that I can answer it on some other occasion, however the answer cannot be a simple yes or no because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question has been withdrawn so therefore in what, how you would answer that question is at this moment not relevant anymore. Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. I want to deal really with only one topic and that's what the purpose of the activity as found by Stevanovic was at Mount Tara.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, P590. I beg your pardon, it's P598.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you just quickly have a look at that document, please, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, this is a document from the 1st Army, an order from the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were you aware of this order, or have you become aware of this order during your work or during your work with the commission?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that in the course of my work I saw a huge number of documents and I can't tell you really precisely whether I've seen this particular document. I did see some comments including some dispatches from the Ministry of the Interior which confirm what is described here in this document, that there were some problems on the border on the Drina River on the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, and from what Mr. Stevanovic told me, the reason that the PJP was actually employed there was specifically to address these incursions that were made and that they -- that had consequences also on the other side of the border in Serbia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. So what Mr. Stevanovic effectively told you was that the Serbian MUP had become involved at Mount Tara in relation to trying to prevent incursions into Serbia, trying to protect the border of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe what the witness believes Mr. Stevanovic effectively told him is irrelevant. What is relevant is what Mr. Stevanovic told him and it should be left for the Chamber to interpret what the meaning of Mr. Stevanovic's words were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. The question was whether Mr. Stevanovic effectively told you that certain things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the question as I see it in the -- there's no asking about what he believed, but what Mr. Stevanovic effectively told the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me -- did you get the question?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Would you like me to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stevanovic told me specifically about Tara. The only thing that he mentioned about the MUP activities on Tara was that all the then secretariats of the Ministry of the Interior had sent one or two of its members for training to -- one of two members of the PJP for training to that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were you also told that the reason for that was that Stevanovic was organising units to patrol the Serb border at a time when the conflict in Bosnia threatened to spill into Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he told me at the time when he met Mr. Simatovic that he had already been engaged with the Uzice Corps on the border towards Drina, but that this was some kind of additional training for specific tasks and these were practically from what we see here, this was really just training for these members and from what we see here it says that one or two members were sent from each of the secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just take a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you tell the Prosecution that this was at a time when the conflict in Bosnia threatened to spill into Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, what I said during that conversation, that was the point, I don't know which words I used specifically. I said the involvement of the PJP along the border to Bosnia in the proximity of Bajina Basta. I said that the reason for their involvement was to prevent any ramifications of the war in Bosnia, any spillover to the Republic of Serbia. There were people who were killed as a result of combat operations in Bosnia who were in Serbia's territory. Until such time as the Army of the Republika Srpska took that territory from the hands of the Bosnian army and then the firing across the Drina stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've got nothing further, thank you. Thank you Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Groome, any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could I ask that D114 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that is being brought up, JF-094, can I ask you the container in Lipovica, is that typical of the way in which other archival material in the possession of the Ministry of the Interior is maintained?

utterances.speaker: JF-094 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you my opinion, but certainly the way in which these documents were kept and the condition in which we found them would not be consistent with the standards applied in archives elsewhere across Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, for those of us who look at this picture and form the opinion that it's an atrocious way to maintain official documents, can you provides some explanation as to how these important records came --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, I mean, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first Mr. Groome completes his question and then you object.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the objection is to Mr. Groome covering this subject at all which hasn't arisen from cross-examination. It's arisen from cross-examination perhaps of the previous witness but not this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was introduced with the last witness and the last witness said I can't speak to this, it's the following witness, so I submit that it's entirely proper for the person with the knowledge about how this occurred to inform us about how these records got into this condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't it true that re-examination is an opportunity to put questions to the witness on matters that were raised or triggered by the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is true, Your Honour, but 90(H) also gives the Chamber some latitude in allowing the parties to address questions to witnesses who have relevant information, and I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is 90(H) dealing with the cross-examining party or with the calling party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Very often with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very often? Could you read the text then, please, for me so that you can convince me that -- you talk about 90(H), isn't it, and you are referring to that a cross-examining party cannot only deal with matters but also can elicit evidence if it supports his case, and I'm now talking from the top of my head, so perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In 90(H)(iii): "The Trial Chamber may, in the exercise of its discretion, permit inquiry into additional matters."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and have you asked for such -- because you were referring to -- the objection was raised on the basis of 90(H), cross-examination shall be limited to subject matter of the evidence in chief and matters affecting credibility and where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party to the subject matter of that case. That apparently was the basis of Mr. Jordash's objection. You, at least from what I understood, were considering the possibility that the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party and then certain rules apply on what shall be put to the witness. (iii), the Trial Chamber may, in the exercise of its discretion, permit inquiry into additional matters. But although all the rest of 90(H) is about the cross-examining party, you consider 90(H) under (iii) to be a general rule which applies to -- not only to cross-examination, and have you asked permission from the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have not asked permission. I have not asked permission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. The Chamber has no further questions for you, witness JF-094. This, therefore, concludes your evidence in this case. I would like to thank you very much for -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it just occurs to me that had this examination proceeded in the ordinary course, that had JF-095 completed his cross-examination and this photograph introduced in the cross-examination, I would have been on notice that -- what the Defence wants to do with this, and I would have certainly in my direct examination of this witness have asked him to explain this. I'm at somewhat of a disadvantage in the procedure adopted by the Chamber. I think it's somewhat unfair of the Defence to introduce the photo without any opportunity for me to elicit from the person who has the most information who is sitting before you his explanation as to what he knows about why it got into this condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if the order would have been opposite, you would have had no opportunity either would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If 94 would have preceded 95?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think I would have made some arguments as to why it wasn't put to the witness before since this is the witness who has information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check with my colleagues

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, this witness -- we have heard evidence that this was not the standard, this was not normal, this was exceptional. If you would argue strongly that the Chamber could not interpret that evidence without knowing exactly why it was exceptional, then we would not disallow you perhaps under those circumstances to ask one question. If, however, you would think that the Chamber would accept that this was the not normal situation, whereas archives are usually kept in a different way, if that would sufficiently assist the Chamber, then you're encouraged not to re-open your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it -- it seems that it will not assist the Chamber, so I will not -- I will decline to ask to re-open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Witness JF-094, I was about to thank you for coming to The Hague and you've shown a great flexibility in being available, which certainly has not been very convenient to you. I would like to thank you very much on behalf of the Chamber for coming, even coming twice, for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Chamber, and I wish you a safe return home again. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Chamber. Your Honours, I'm available to this Tribunal whenever necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that offer. Could you please follow the usher who will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I finally address you, Mr. Cvetkovic and Mr. Ignjatovic, apart from one small moment where there was perhaps a matter which would have needed further discussion, apart from that I think the examination of the witnesses went smoothly. It was a pleasure for the Chamber to have you present and I wish you the same, that is a safe journey home again, whether it's close or further away. Thank you. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I earlier informed the parties that the Chamber would like to have an out-of-court meeting with the parties in order to put an end to not-too-well organised situations. The Chamber would also like to use that, unless the parties would consider it inappropriate to discuss it anywhere else than in the courtroom, the practicalities of the request for a postponement of the testimony of Mr. Theunens. The reason why I would like to include that is not to have full argument on that request or motion but to see whether the Chamber could assist the parties in finding a solution for what apparently is a problem. I have on my mind to have such a meeting on Thursday, further details to be made known to the parties, but we still need a place to meet. Is there any objection against, apart from the other matter I just raised, to also see whether the Chamber can assist the parties in finding a solution for the scheduling of witness Theunens? If there are no objections, we stand adjourned and we resume tomorrow Tuesday, the 14th of September, quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
